places.quote: don't treat the model as a black box — check its CV and percentiles against the data; occurrences, and frequency and severity, are assumed independent; numerical methods can err at low frequencies; and the model captures process variance but not parameter variance or model risk.

requirements.statement: The damage function (damage ratio curve) in a catastrophe model gives the mean damage ratio (damage as a fraction of the property's value) as a function of event intensity at the site.

places.quote: *vulnerability* (damage given intensity)

requirements.statement: Uncertainty in the damage function is represented by a distribution of damage ratios around the mean at each given intensity (secondary uncertainty in damage).

places.quote: Even for a given event the loss is uncertain, because damage to buildings of the same type varies. Models carry a distribution of loss for each event, often a beta distribution, and including it fattens the tail of the curves while leaving the AAL unchanged.

requirements.statement: Uncertainty in the intensity experienced at the site, given an earthquake (e.g., from an initial estimate of intensity), is represented by a probability distribution over intensity (secondary uncertainty in hazard).

Event loss at a given intensity equals the damage ratio read from the damage function times the property value; expected annual loss is the probability-weighted sum of these losses over the possible events.

places.quote: $$\text{AAL} = \sum_{i} \lambda_i\, \bar{L}_i$$
$$\text{AAL} = \sum_i \lambda_i\,\bar L_i$$

requirements.statement: The standard deviation of loss over discrete events is the square root of (sum of probability times loss squared minus the squared expected loss), with the no-event outcome contributing zero loss.
requirements.concept: Variance and Standard Deviation of Discrete Distribution

requirements.statement: Risk load is a specified percentage multiplied by the standard deviation of loss (standard deviation risk load).

places.quote: *standard deviation*: $P = E[X] + k\,\sigma(X)$
the standard deviation principle $E[X] + k\,\sigma(X)$ and the variance principle $E[X] + k\,\text{Var}(X)$

requirements.statement: With an expense load expressed as a percentage of premium, premium = (expected loss + risk load) / (1 − expense load percentage).

The chi-square statistic for testing shifting risk parameters is the sum over groups of (actual - expected)^2 / expected, where expected counts equal exposure times the overall mean frequency (equivalently, exposure-weighted squared frequency deviations divided by the overall frequency).
requirements.concept: Chi-Square Test for Shifting Risk Parameters

requirements.statement: Compare the chi-square statistic to the critical value at the given significance level with degrees of freedom equal to the number of groups minus one; reject the null of no shift if the statistic exceeds the critical value.
requirements.concept: Chi-Square Test for Shifting Risk Parameters

places.quote: Reject $H_0$ at level $\alpha$ when $Q$ exceeds the upper-$\alpha$ [[Critical Value|critical value]] of the [[Chi-Squared Distribution|chi-squared distribution]] with $k - 1 - r$ degrees of freedom.

requirements.statement: When exposures are not given, use earned premium as the exposure base, test each line separately, and compute expected counts as each group's premium times the overall claim frequency per premium.

To evaluate a credibility weight Z with the MSE criterion, form for each past period a prediction as Z/2 times each of the two prior periods' frequencies plus (1-Z) times the cumulative overall frequency up to that point, then average the squared differences between actual and predicted frequencies; choose the Z with the lowest MSE.
The credibility-weighted frequency estimate is the sum of Z-weighted recent-period frequencies plus (1-Z) times the overall mean frequency.
requirements.concept: Limited Fluctuation and Greatest Accuracy Credibility

places.quote: $$\text{Estimate} = Z \times \text{Experience} + (1 - Z) \times \text{Complement}$$
$$\text{Estimate} = Z \cdot \bar{X} + (1 - Z)\cdot \mu_0$$
$$\text{Estimate} = Z \cdot \bar{X} + (1-Z) \cdot \mu_0$$

requirements.statement: Aggregate excess of loss ceded premium is rate on line times the limit, and the ceded loss is the gross aggregate loss in excess of the attachment, capped at the limit; ceded profit is ceded premium minus ceded loss.

places.quote: $$Y = \min\left(\max(S - A,\, 0),\; L_A\right)$$
*rate on line* $=$ premium $\div L$; *payback* $= L \div$ premium, in years.
$$\text{Ceded}_{\text{Agg}} = \min\left(\max(S - A,\,0),\; L_A\right)$$

requirements.statement: For an aggregate quota share, ceded premium and ceded loss are the cession percentage of gross premium and loss, with ceded loss limited by the loss ratio cap. Ceded profit equals ceded premium minus ceding commission, ceded loss and any profit commission, where the profit commission returns to the cedent the excess of the target profit over zero margin (the amount by which profit exceeds the target percent of ceded premium).
requirements.concept: Quota Share Reinsurance with Profit Commission

places.quote: $$\begin{aligned} \text{Ceded premium} &= a \cdot P \\ \text{Ceded loss} &= a \cdot X \end{aligned}$$
$$\text{PC} = k \times \max\left(0,\; 1 - \text{LR} - c - m\right)$$
$$\text{Commission} = c \times \text{Ceded premium}$$

requirements.statement: The reinsurer's expected combined ratio equals the expected loss ratio plus the ceding commission, brokerage, administrative and unallocated expense ratios, so the target loss ratio is the target combined ratio minus all expense ratios.
requirements.concept: Reinsurance Pricing: Combined Ratio and Expenses

places.quote: $$\text{Reinsurer's ratio} = \text{ELR} + c + b + e$$
$$\text{Target LR} = 1 - V - F - Q$$

requirements.statement: A loss corridor is a reinsurance provision under which the ceding insurer reassumes a specified percentage of losses falling between two loss ratios (the corridor), reducing the reinsurer's losses in that band.

places.quote: **A Loss Corridor** is a reinsurance contract provision under which the cedant **reassumes** part of the reinsurer's liability when the treaty loss ratio falls within a stated band.
*Loss corridor:* the cedant reassumes losses in a band of loss ratios, which lowers the reinsurer's expected loss even when the expected loss ratio is below the band.

requirements.statement: Compute the expected loss ratio from a loss ratio distribution as the probability-weighted sum of the average loss ratios in each range.
requirements.concept: Expected Loss Ratio from Loss Ratio Distribution

places.quote: $$E\left[g(\text{LR})\right] = \sum_i p_i \, g(\text{LR}_i)$$
$$E[c] = \sum_i p_i \, c(\text{LR}_i)$$

requirements.statement: The loss ratio reassumed in a corridor for a given outcome is the corridor share times the portion of the loss ratio within the corridor: zero below the lower bound, the excess over the lower bound inside the corridor, and the full corridor width above the upper bound.

places.quote: $$\text{LR}_{\text{net}} = \text{LR} - c \cdot \min\left(\max(\text{LR} - a,\, 0),\; b - a\right)$$
Reassumed points $0.5\min(\max(\text{LR} - 80, 0), 20)$: $0, 0, 5, 10$.

requirements.statement: To find the reassumed corridor percentage, set the expected loss ratio net of corridor recoveries (expected unadjusted loss ratio minus the expected corridor loss ratio times the share) equal to the target loss ratio, and solve for the share, equivalently dividing the required loss ratio reduction by the expected loss ratio within the corridor.

A probable maximum loss (PML) at a given return period is the loss on the exceedance probability curve whose annual exceedance probability equals the reciprocal of the return period (e.g., 1-in-N corresponds to EP = 1/N).

places.quote: **The Probable Maximum Loss** (PML) is the loss an insurer's portfolio would suffer from a catastrophe of a specified return period
$$\text{Return period}(x) = \frac{1}{\text{EP}(x)}$$

requirements.statement: To find a PML at a return period not listed in the table, convert return periods to exceedance probabilities and linearly interpolate between the bracketing points on exceedance probability, not on return period years.
Apply an excess-of-loss layer to a gross loss: ceded loss is the portion of the gross loss above the attachment point, capped at the layer limit, and net loss is gross minus ceded.

places.quote: the reinsurer pays the part of each loss — per risk or per occurrence — above the cedant's retention $R$ (the attachment point), up to a limit $L$.
applies $\min(\max(X - R, 0), L)$ to projected ultimates of large claims.

requirements.statement: An occurrence exceedance probability (OEP) curve describes the largest single event loss in a year, whereas an aggregate exceedance probability (AEP) curve describes total annual losses; per-occurrence treaty terms are applied to an OEP basis.
requirements.concept: Occurrence and Aggregate Exceedance Probability Curves

places.quote: The *occurrence* curve (OEP) looks at the largest single event in a year, the *aggregate* curve (AEP) at the year's total.
The occurrence exceedance probability is the chance that the largest single event in a year exceeds $x$, which is what a per-occurrence [[Excess of Loss|excess of loss]] treaty responds to.

requirements.statement: PMLs for a portfolio are not additive across contracts or perils; the combined PML must be assessed by re-running the model on the combined portfolio, because the 1-in-N events for different perils do not coincide.

places.quote: Model-based portfolio management judges each new account by its *marginal* effect $\Delta\rho$ on the portfolio's AAL and tail, not by its stand-alone loss.
When risks are aggregated, the capital needed for the [[Portfolio|portfolio]] is less than the sum of the capital each would need alone

requirements.statement: Writing a contract exposed to a different peril than the one driving the existing PML provides diversification benefit, so the reinsurer's required capital for the 1-in-N standard rises by less than the contract's standalone PML.

places.quote: An account in an unrelated region can add little to the portfolio's tail; the same account in the peak zone adds a great deal, and should be priced or declined accordingly
**Risk diversification** is the reduction in total risk that comes from holding risks that don't all reach their worst outcomes at the same time.

requirements.statement: A reinsurer's capital requirement is that its capital must cover its 1-in-N PML (the survival standard), so a new contract is acceptable if the resulting combined PML stays within available capital.
requirements.concept: Reinsurer Capital Adequacy and Risk Tolerance

places.quote: net PML — after reinsurance and after any reinstatement premiums — is what actually hits capital. OSFI's earthquake requirements test whether the insurer's financial resources cover the net exposure.
A [[Risk Appetite|risk appetite]] typically caps a net PML or TVaR as a share of surplus, with capacity limits for peak zones.

requirements.statement: The inventory module of a catastrophe model describes the properties at risk (location, construction type, and other characteristics of the insured exposures).

places.quote: the exposed properties (construction type, building codes, built value, contents)
*inventory* (the exposed properties)

requirements.statement: The vulnerability module of a catastrophe model quantifies the physical damage to properties at risk from a given hazard intensity, i.e. the susceptibility of building types to damage, often via damage functions developed using engineering judgment, building response analysis, or claims data.

places.quote: *vulnerability* (damage given intensity)

requirements.statement: A change in a building's construction characteristics affects both the inventory module (to identify the new construction type in the portfolio) and the vulnerability module (to reflect its changed damage susceptibility).

places.quote: Grossi and Kunreuther describe a catastrophe model in four parts: *hazard* (where events occur, how often, how intense), *inventory* (the exposed properties), *vulnerability* (damage given intensity) and *loss* (the financial result after policy terms).

requirements.statement: Aleatory uncertainty is the inherent randomness of the hazard event itself (process risk), while epistemic uncertainty stems from lack of knowledge or data (parameter risk) and can be reduced with more scientific knowledge.
requirements.concept: Sources of Uncertainty in Catastrophe Models

places.quote: *Aleatory* uncertainty is the inherent randomness of events and cannot be reduced; *epistemic* uncertainty comes from incomplete knowledge of the hazard, vulnerability and exposure, and can be.

requirements.statement: Uncertainty about the effectiveness of a new, untested technique with no historical performance data and no expert consensus is epistemic uncertainty, since it arises from lack of knowledge rather than inherent randomness.
requirements.concept: Sources of Uncertainty in Catastrophe Models

places.quote: *Aleatory* uncertainty is the inherent randomness of events and cannot be reduced; *epistemic* uncertainty comes from incomplete knowledge of the hazard, vulnerability and exposure, and can be.

requirements.statement: A logic tree incorporates uncertainty by assigning probability weights (based on expert opinion) to alternative parameter values or model branches and combining the results as a weighted average; it is easy to trace and communicate but relies on subjective, simplified opinions and does not scale well to many scenarios.

Simulation incorporates uncertainty by randomly sampling parameter values from probability distributions over many trials to produce a distribution of outcomes; it handles complex situations and richer assumptions but is computationally intensive and can be a black box.

places.quote: A simulation draws the parameter and *then* the outcome for each iteration, and ranks the outcomes.

requirements.statement: A sliding-scale commission varies the ceding commission inversely with the loss ratio, between a minimum commission at a high loss ratio and a maximum commission at a low loss ratio, with a stated slide rate (e.g., 1:1 or 0.5:1) in each interval.

places.quote: A Sliding Scale Commission is a ceding commission on a proportional treaty that varies inversely with the treaty's actual loss ratio, between a stated minimum and maximum.
A sliding scale commission moves with the treaty's loss experience between a minimum and a maximum.

requirements.statement: To find the commission for a given loss ratio, start at the commission at the nearest scale breakpoint and adjust by the slide rate times the loss ratio difference within that interval, capped at the minimum and maximum commission.

places.quote: c(\text{LR}) = \min\left(c_{\max},\; \max\left(c_{\min},\; c_0 + s\,(\text{LR}_0 - \text{LR})\right)\right)

requirements.statement: The reinsurer's technical ratio is the expected loss ratio plus the ceding commission ratio (plus other expense loads), representing the reinsurer's cost relative to premium.

places.quote: \text{Reinsurer's ratio} = \text{ELR} + c + b + e

requirements.statement: A carry-forward provision in a sliding-scale commission lets loss ratio experience above the minimum-commission loss ratio (the excess not already reflected in minimum commission) be added to the next year's loss ratio when computing that year's commission.

places.quote: Past deficits above the minimum-commission loss ratio can be carried into the current year.
A deficit (negative profit) in one year is often carried into the next year's calculation.

requirements.statement: To value a carry-forward, compute the expected carry-forward amount from year 1 (probability-weighted loss ratio excess over the minimum-commission loss ratio), add it to year 2 loss ratios for commission calculation, and weight year 2 results by scenarios with and without carry-forward.

places.quote: Priced for a single year, this simply shifts the slide by the carryforward.
either shift the terms by the carryforward, or model a multi-year block with reduced variance.
The carryforward halves year 2's payment, so the reinsurer recovers part of year 1's loss before sharing year 2's profit.

requirements.statement: The expected technical ratio over a loss distribution is the probability-weighted average of the technical ratios (or loss ratios plus commissions) of the loss ratio ranges, using the average loss ratio within each range.

places.quote: E[c] = \sum_i p_i \, c(\text{LR}_i)
Tabulate ranges of the loss ratio with each range's probability and average loss ratio, evaluate the provision in each range, and weight.

requirements.statement: Experience loss cost for an excess layer is estimated by averaging historical on-level trended layer loss costs (per unit of subject premium), weighted by on-level subject premium (a simple average is also acceptable).

places.quote: An [[Excess of Loss|excess of loss]] layer gets its loss cost from **experience rating**, the *burning cost*: trended, developed layer losses over on-level subject premium.
Sum the layer losses by year, apply *excess* development factors (the layer reports and develops later than gross), and divide by [[On Level Premium|on-level]] subject premium.

requirements.statement: An exposure curve G(x) gives the proportion of total (ground-up) pure risk premium that falls below a loss size x expressed as a fraction of the maximum possible loss; the share in a layer is G(upper/max) minus G(attachment/max).

places.quote: **Exposure Curves** give, for a class of property risks, the share of expected loss that falls below a retention expressed as a fraction $d$ of each risk's maximum possible loss.
For property, use an [[Exposure Curves|exposure curve]]: $G\big((R+L)/IV\big) - G\big(R/IV\big)$ by insured-value band.

requirements.statement: Exposure-rated layer loss cost equals the expected subject loss ratio (pure risk premium ratio) times the exposure curve's layer share, with the subject loss ratio computed net of quota share when the quota share inures to the excess treaty.

places.quote: $\text{EF}$ times subject premium times the expected loss ratio is the layer loss ([[Limited Expected Value]]).
In both cases the factor multiplies subject premium times the expected loss ratio.

requirements.statement: Experience and exposure loss cost estimates are combined as a credibility-weighted average: Z times the experience estimate plus (1 − Z) times the exposure estimate.
requirements.concept: Credibility Weighting of Experience and Exposure Rating

places.quote: $$\text{Estimate} = Z \times \text{Experience} + (1 - Z) \times \text{Complement}$$

requirements.statement: Ceded premium for an excess treaty equals expected ceded losses divided by the ceded loss ratio; ceded loss equals loss cost times subject premium.
requirements.concept: Reinsurance Pricing: Ceded Premium and Loss Ratio

places.quote: $$\text{Loss cost} = \frac{E[\text{Ceded loss}]}{\text{Subject premium}}$$
Ceded premium is $0.40 \times \$50\text{M} = \$20$ million and expected ceded loss is $0.672 \times \$20\text{M} = \$13.44$ million.

requirements.statement: Insurer's net underwriting profit after reinsurance = gross premium + ceding commission received − premium ceded (quota share and excess) − net retained losses (gross losses less ceded recoveries) − expenses; a quota share inuring to the excess treaty means the excess subject premium is net of the quota share, and gross premium is net premium divided by (1 − QS%).

places.quote: $$\text{Net} = \text{Gross} - \text{Ceded}$$
$$\text{Commission} = c \times \text{Ceded premium}$$

requirements.statement: A quota share cedes a fixed percentage of premium and losses to the reinsurer, and the reinsurer pays the cedent a ceding commission as a percentage of ceded premium.

places.quote: **Quota Share** is a proportional treaty in which the reinsurer takes a fixed percentage $a$ of the premium and of every loss (usually including ALAE) on a defined book. In return it pays the cedant a **ceding commission** for the expenses the cedant incurred to write the business.
$$\text{Commission} = c \times \text{Ceded premium}$$

requirements.statement: Profit commission each year = profit-commission % × max(0, 1 − ceded loss ratio − ceding commission − reinsurer margin), applied to ceded premium and floored at zero for each year separately; the multi-year ratio is the premium-weighted average (total profit commission divided by total ceded premium).

places.quote: $$\text{PC} = k \times \max\left(0,\; 1 - \text{LR} - c - m\right)$$

requirements.statement: A profit commission is variable and pays only when results are favorable (rewards good underwriting/risk control, but is less stable and may pay less in expectation), while a higher flat ceding commission is guaranteed and paid upfront.

places.quote: It is paid only when that profit is positive, so the cedant shares the upside and never the downside.

requirements.statement: The return period of a loss level is the average number of years between exceedances of that level; a 1-in-N year return period corresponds to an annual exceedance probability of 1/N.

places.quote: A $1$-in-$500$ event has a $0.2\%$ annual probability; over $30$ years the probability of at least one such event is $1 - 0.998^{30} \approx 5.8\%$.
$$\text{Return period}(x) = \frac{1}{\text{EP}(x)}$$
A 1-in-100 loss has a 1% chance each year, not a guarantee of occurring once a century.

requirements.statement: To find the probability that retained loss exceeds a given amount, read the return period at that loss level off the exceedance curve (loss by return period) and take its reciprocal.

places.quote: The year's total exceeds $70$ once in $1/0.005 = 200$ years.
A [[Probable Maximum Loss|probable maximum loss]] is the loss at a stated return period, a value-at-risk read off the OEP or AEP curve.

requirements.statement: A quota share treaty cedes the same fixed proportion of every loss, so the retained loss distribution is the gross distribution scaled down by a constant; the coefficient of variation of retained and ceded loss therefore equals that of gross loss.

places.quote: Net loss is $(1-a)X$, so its coefficient of variation equals gross.
Because every policy is shared alike, a quota share reduces the cedant's net premium and net losses in proportion without changing the shape of its results.

requirements.statement: The quota share percentage equals 1 minus the ratio of retained loss to gross loss at any given return period (equivalently, 1 minus retained AAL divided by gross AAL).

places.quote: Net loss is $(1-a)X$, so its coefficient of variation equals gross.
**Symbols:** $X$ is a loss and $a$ is the quota share percentage ceded.

requirements.statement: A reinsurance layer with a higher coefficient of variation of ceded loss (more volatile, tail-focused coverage) carries more uncertainty and requires more reinsurer capital, so the reinsurer charges a higher risk load in the premium.

places.quote: *standard deviation*: $P = E[X] + k\,\sigma(X)$ — the load scales with share, so a 50% share pays half;

Catastrophe business also consumes a great deal of capital, so a separate [[Risk Loads|risk load]] is added — commonly tied to the modelled volatility or to the capital (the [[Probable Maximum Loss|PML]] or tail measure) the exposure draws on.

requirements.statement: A tranche in a CDO pool absorbs losses in order of seniority: the junior tranche takes the first slice of loss, the mezzanine the next slice, and the senior only after those are exhausted, so a tranche defaults when pool losses exceed the attachment point below it.

places.quote: The tranche loses nothing until the claims beneath it are exhausted, then absorbs everything up to its size $d - a$.

requirements.statement: With perfectly correlated defaults, all bonds in the pool default together, so the probability that the pool suffers any given level of loss equals the single-bond default probability.

places.quote: At $\rho = 1$ the structure achieves no enhancement at all.

requirements.statement: With independent (uncorrelated) defaults, the number of defaulting bonds is binomial, and the probability a tranche defaults is the probability that the number of defaults is enough to push losses past that tranche's lower attachment point (computed directly or as one minus the complement).

places.quote: With $N \sim \text{Bin}(10, p)$ defaults, equity is impaired if $N \geq 1$, mezzanine if $N \geq 2$, senior if $N \geq 4$.
The **Binomial Distribution** $X \sim \text{Bin}(n, p)$ models the number of successes in $n$ independent Bernoulli trials, each with probability of success $p$.

requirements.statement: Underestimating default probabilities (and ignoring correlation) made senior CDO tranches appear very safe, so rating agencies gave them AAA ratings, which made them attractive to investors through yield advantage and lower capital requirements, driving the rise of structured finance.

places.quote: so it is acutely sensitive to **default [[Correlation|correlation]]** and to errors in default probabilities and recoveries.

requirements.statement: When underlying defaults rose above the estimated levels, the CDO structure magnified the effect of the underestimation, so senior tranches suffered losses and downgrades despite AAA ratings, and investors lost trust in structured finance, causing its fall.

places.quote: Coval, Jurek & Stafford's first point is that tranching **amplifies** those errors, and re-tranching tranches (the CDO-squared) amplifies them again.
Coval, Jurek & Stafford's AAA senior tranche falls to A+ at a correlation of 40% and to BBB− at 60%

requirements.statement: A CAT bond's limit is fully collateralized (investor funds are held in a trust via the special purpose reinsurer), so the issuer faces essentially no counterparty default (credit) risk.

places.quote: A cat bond's principal is held in a collateral trust, largely removing counterparty credit risk.
use fully collateralised capacity such as [[CAT Bonds]], which protects the cedant from the reinsurer's default, though a bond on a trigger other than the cedant's own losses leaves it basis risk.

requirements.statement: A catastrophe risk swap is an unfunded agreement to pay on a covered event, so each party is exposed to counterparty default risk that can be reduced by choosing a financially strong counterparty.
Basis risk is the risk that the payoff from a risk transfer instrument does not match the insurer's actual loss; it is driven by the trigger rather than by the other party's catastrophe exposure.

places.quote: **Basis risk** — the gap between the sponsor's actual loss and its recovery — is two-sided, and it has an accounting consequence: a non-indemnity bond may not qualify as reinsurance.

Its trigger — indemnity (the sponsor's own losses), industry index, parametric (physical event measures) or modelled loss — trades *basis risk* (the payout not matching the sponsor's loss) against moral hazard, transparency and speed of settlement.
though a bond on a trigger other than the cedant's own losses leaves it basis risk.

requirements.statement: Trigger types (indemnity, index, parametric) determine basis risk: indemnity triggers have the least basis risk but are less liked by investors, while index and parametric triggers carry more basis risk. The trigger is chosen in both CAT bonds and CAT risk swaps, so both can limit basis risk if structured appropriately.

places.quote: **Triggers** — indemnity at one end (no basis risk, the most moral hazard) and parametric at the other (the most basis risk), with modelled-loss and industry-index triggers between:
index or parametric triggers trade moral hazard for **basis risk**.

requirements.statement: A CAT bond acts like excess-of-loss reinsurance and gives the issuing company no risk diversification; the diversification benefit (catastrophe risk uncorrelated with investment returns) accrues to the investors.

places.quote: Because [[Catastrophe Risk|catastrophe losses]] are nearly independent of financial markets, investors value that return as a diversifier.

places.quote: Idiosyncratic defaults diversify away in a large pool, so a senior tranche is impaired only in a severe, economy-wide downturn.

CAT bonds are fully collateralized (no credit risk), often have multi-year pricing locks and lower margins and transaction costs, and cat risk is uncorrelated with financial markets so investors accept lower spreads, making them attractive for high layers where reinsurer credit risk and price are concerns.

places.quote: **CAT Bonds** (catastrophe bonds) are fully collateralised securities through which an insurer or reinsurer — the **sponsor** — buys multi-year catastrophe protection from capital-market investors.
collateral replaces a reinsurer's promise, so there is no [[Reinsurance Credit Risk|credit risk]] on the limit

places.quote: indemnity at one end (no basis risk, the most moral hazard) and parametric at the other (the most basis risk)

places.quote: **Industry index** — an industry loss estimate (PCS in the U.S.). Transparent and quick; basis risk wherever the sponsor's book differs from the industry's.

places.quote: Written as reinsurance they add a second trigger on the buyer's own loss, which supplies the indemnity.

requirements.statement: In the insurance CAPM (Cummins, corrected), a line's required underwriting return as a percentage of premium is r_i = -(k_i/s_i) r_F + β_i (r_M - r_F), where k_i is liabilities to equity and s_i is premium to equity.

places.quote: $$\text{UPM} = -k\,R_f + \beta_u\big[E(R_m) - R_f\big]$$

requirements.statement: The ratio k_i/s_i equals liabilities divided by premium (L_i/P_i), so the risk-free interest credit on policyholder-supplied funds must be expressed per dollar of premium rather than per dollar of equity.

Because the insurer earns the risk-free rate on policyholder-supplied funds, the required underwriting return is reduced by that investment credit (a negative term), so the line can be priced at an expected underwriting loss while still giving owners their required return.

places.quote: Fairley's model gives the insurer the risk-free rate on the premium it holds, $-k\,R_f$, plus a premium for systematic underwriting risk, $\beta_u\big[E(R_m) - R_f\big]$.

In long-tailed lines (personal auto bodily injury, workers compensation) years may pass between the premium and the settlement of all claims, and the investment income can be large enough to accept an underwriting loss and still achieve the target total return;

requirements.statement: Policyholders are charged only for the line's systematic (market-related) underwriting risk, measured by underwriting beta times the market risk premium (r_M - r_F).

places.quote: In practice underwriting betas are hard to estimate, and the CAPM prices only systematic risk, whereas an insurer's frictional costs depend on *total* risk — including the diversifiable risk the CAPM treats as free.

requirements.statement: The PSA prepayment benchmark expresses prepayment speed as a conditional prepayment rate (CPR) that rises linearly with pool age (100% PSA is 0.2% per month of age up to 6% at month 30, then level), and a quoted PSA percentage is a multiple of this benchmark CPR.

places.quote: 100% PSA assumes a CPR of 0.2% in the first month, rising by 0.2% a month to 6% at month 30 and level after that. A pool is quoted as a multiple of it, such as 150 PSA, rather than as a model of borrower behavior.

requirements.statement: The conditional prepayment rate (CPR) is an annualized rate of prepayment on the pool's remaining balance, while the single monthly mortality rate (SMM) is the corresponding monthly prepayment rate.

places.quote: SMM (single monthly mortality) is the fraction of the balance left after the month's scheduled principal that is prepaid in the month; CPR (conditional prepayment rate) is its annualised equivalent, so $\text{SMM} = 1 - (1 - \text{CPR})^{1/12}$.

requirements.statement: The monthly prepayment rate is obtained from the annual CPR by compounding conversion: SMM = 1 - (1 - CPR)^(1/12).

places.quote: SMM (single monthly mortality) is the fraction of the balance left after the month's scheduled principal that is prepaid in the month; CPR (conditional prepayment rate) is its annualised equivalent, so $\text{SMM} = 1 - (1 - \text{CPR})^{1/12}$.

requirements.statement: Expected monthly prepayment equals SMM multiplied by the beginning-of-month balance after subtracting that month's scheduled principal payment.

places.quote: The SMM applies to the balance after the month's scheduled principal.

requirements.statement: Aggregate capital under a correlation matrix (square-root formula) equals the square root of the sum over all ordered pairs (i, j) of Corr_{i,j} × C_i × C_j, where C_i are the standalone risk capitals.

places.quote: $$C = \sqrt{\sum_i \sum_j \rho_{ij}\, C_i\, C_j}$$

requirements.statement: Because the correlation matrix is symmetric and the diagonal entries equal 1, the double sum equals the sum of squared capitals plus twice the sum of each distinct pair's cross term.

places.quote: Each pair appears twice in the double sum, so the cross term is $2\rho_{ij} C_i C_j$.

requirements.statement: Aggregate capital is less than the sum of standalone capitals when correlations are below 1; the difference is the diversification credit, and the sum of standalone capitals corresponds to perfect correlation.

places.quote: A simple sum assumes every correlation is one, which gives no benefit and an upper bound.
Adding the margins together assumes perfect correlation; the credit removes part of that over-statement.

requirements.statement: With all correlations equal to zero (independent risks), aggregate capital is the square root of the sum of squared standalone capitals, giving the largest diversification credit.

places.quote: the square root treats $R_1$–$R_5$ and $R_{\text{cat}}$ as independent.
Most formulas add some charges in full and combine the rest by a square root, which assumes the main risks are independent or correlated by a set matrix.
